transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-13
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Malhotra (Starlane Head of Cloud), Ethan Suarez (Infra Lead), Nina Park (Partnerships)

Auto-summary (auto generated, may be imperfect):
- Quick intros, outline of resell/pilot partnership options
- Discussion of technical compatibility for private VPC and on-prem GPU pools; network egress and peering questions
- Pilot of ~6 weeks to validate throughput and cost per token on sample workloads
- Next steps: SOW, benchmarks, legal/compliance contacts

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. um quick roll call?
[00:06] Priya (Starlane): Hi, Priya here.
[00:08] Ethan (Starlane): Ethan.
[00:10] Nina (Starlane): Nina here.
[00:12] Liam (Redwood SE): Liam here — thanks.
[00:15] Maya: Cool. We'll keep this to about 45-60 mins, background first: Redwood's partner/reseller program and typical pilot flow, then technical Qs.

[01:02] Maya: Starlane, just to ground us — can you give a quick overview of your managed GPU offering, fleet size, and target customers?
[01:12] Priya: Sure, so Starlane operates a managed GPU cluster across two regions, US-east and eu-west. Right now our fleet is mostly A800s and some V100s in legacy racks, and we're pushing a refreshed pool with H100s later this quarter. We sell to ML SaaS companies who want a private managed inference environment — many customers ask for a turnkey on-prem gateway or a VPC peering arrangement.
[01:45] Ethan: From infra side, our key constraints are cross-AZ bandwidth, strict egress controls, and a multi-tenant hyperplane we run on top of K8s. We also have some customers that require air-gapped installs.

[02:18] Maya: Great — that aligns with a lot of our partners. High level, Redwood supports three deployment modes: hosted, dedicated, and private (VPC/on-prem). For a reseller model you can either route customers to Redwood-hosted with a reseller margin, or run Redwood Private inside your customers' VPCs or on Starlane-managed infra.
[02:48] Priya: When you say Redwood Private, is that a control plane that runs in our network and talk to your runtime, or everything is customer side? Just trying to map security boundaries.

[03:05] Liam (SE): Good question. Redwood Private can be deployed in a couple of ways. There's a customer-managed control plane option — that sits in your VPC and talks to our support/control plane for telemetry and lifecycle ops, or we can ship an air-gapped package where the control plane is fully on-prem. The inference runtime (the GPUs) stays in the customer's environment in both cases. The control-plane talk includes encrypted metrics and can be configured to use customer KMS.
[03:39] Ethan: KMS integration is important — our enterprise customers require HSM-backed keys and rotation policies.
[03:45] Liam: We have KMS/HSM integrations and can support customer-managed keys. There might be a small handshake for onboarding the key material but it's supported.

[04:03] Nina: On the commercial side, how do margins work for resellers? Do you have a published partner price or is it custom?
[04:11] Maya: We have a partner tier structure. For initial pilots we typically provide a discounted pilot rate and then a reseller discount during contract. I'll follow up with the reseller margin sheet — it's not in the deck right now.

[04:30] Priya: Cool. Also curious about model versioning and compatibility. Our customers run different LLMs — open models, some fine-tuned variants. How flexible is Redwood with custom model artifacts?
[04:45] Liam: Redwood's runtime supports custom model artifacts and a model catalog. We do validate ONNX/PEFT/checkpoint formats at onboarding; there are a few edge cases with custom ops where we need to compile kernels. For quantized models we have recommended quant profiles, and for some third-party ops we may need to do a small compatibility shim.
[05:09] Ethan: What about KV cache and stateful sessions for chat? Our customers expect multi-turn contexts and low latency.
[05:18] Liam: We handle KV cache natively in the runtime. There are two common patterns: keep the cache server-side inside the runtime for low-latency sessions, or let customers host the cache with a shared store — depends on security. For low latency prioritized tenants we recommend the in-runtime cache. There's also automated prefix caching that can reduce tokens for repeated prompts.
[05:47] Priya: Nice — that prefix cache is attractive. Do you support batching with strict per-tenant isolation? We can't mix workloads across customers in our multi-tenant offering.
[05:58] Liam: Yes, tenant-aware batching is built in — batches are formed with isolation boundaries so tokens aren't intermingled. We also expose batching/window configs per-tenant so you can tune latency vs throughput.

[06:24] Maya: Let's talk pilot sizing. Typical pilot we propose is 4–8 weeks: onboarding, a small production-like benchmark, and then a real-customer integration test. What are Starlane's success criteria?
[06:37] Priya: For us, success is threefold: 1) Clear throughput & latency numbers on H100s vs our baseline, 2) Smooth key management + SSO/SAML integration, and 3) a commercial path where we can justify a margin for resale. If the pilot shows >20% cost improvement or better latency at parity, we can push to an initial 10-customer roll.
[07:06] Maya: Good. We'll propose specific SLAs and a benchmark matrix. We'll likely suggest latency P95 at target prompt lengths and tokens-per-sec throughput for your model mix.

[07:25] [Speaker 3]: um, can you support function call style outputs or structured tool calls? Some of our customers use agent-like patterns.
[07:33] Liam: Yes, Redwood supports streaming responses, function/tool calling, and structured outputs. We also have tensor-friendly I/O for embeddings and reranking. There might be some small work to validate toolhub integrations but it's standard.

[08:00] Ethan: Networking — if we run Redwood Private in a customer's VPC, what's the control-plane egress? We have strict outbound firewall rules.
[08:10] Liam: Control plane endpoints are fixed IP ranges and we can support peered VPC connections. For air-gapped installs, the control plane isn't required. For telemetry-only modes you can restrict egress to a single collector. We'll share the CIDR ranges and port list.

[08:38] Nina: On legal/compliance: SOC2 is a must for our customers. Do you have that?
[08:45] Maya: Redwood is SOC2 Type II certified; we also support audit logs, per-request tracing, and can produce evidence for compliance teams. For some customers we also do tailored contracts with additional data residency clauses.

[09:05] Priya: Good. Are there any reseller exclusivity terms? Some partners ask for territory or vertical exclusives.
[09:12] Maya: We generally avoid exclusives in early pilots; later on we can discuss go-to-market co-sell agreements with carve-outs. For now we'll keep it non-exclusive.

[09:30] Ethan: Deep technical question: model compilation and kernel selection — if we have different sequence length distributions and large batch windows, will the runtime choose suboptimal kernels for some workloads?

[09:45] Liam: The runtime has a kernel selection layer that picks implementations based on model arch, sequence lengths, and hardware. We also perform offline tuning — you can feed us a sample prompt distribution and we'll generate an optimized profile. In rare cases a custom kernel may be required but that's uncommon for standard LLMs.

[10:15] Priya: Sounds good. For the pilot, we'll need a quick perf/price comparison vs our current stack — is it okay to run side-by-side benchmarks?

[10:25] Maya: Absolutely. That's exactly what we expect. Liam will propose a benchmark suite and a small dataset; we'll instrument tracing and cost per token breakdowns.

[10:40] [00:10:40] Liam: Quick note on instrumentation: we expose token-level cost estimates, per-route latency breakdowns, and KV cache hit-rate metrics. We can push those to your observability endpoint or give you a dashboard in the Redwood Console.

[11:05] Ethan: Dashboard is good. We need per-tenant billing to map to users as well.
[11:10] Maya: We can tag tokens/requests per-customer and produce exportable usage files.

[11:25] Nina: On integration complexity — how much work is typical for Starlane to onboard a given customer to Redwood Private? Which parts are the high friction bits?

[11:35] Liam: From our experience, onboarding effort centers on a) network connectivity & firewall rules b) key material and SSO integration c) validating custom model artifacts. Each usually takes a few days to a couple of weeks depending on customer resources. For many partners we offer an onboarding concierge to accelerate it.

[12:00] Priya: Do you have a partner SDK or terraform modules so Starlane can template installs for customers?

[12:08] Maya: Yes, we have terraform modules and an operator for K8s that most partners use. We'll share the repo links. For air-gapped customers we also have an install playbook.

[12:28] Ethan: Latency SLA question: some of our customers need <50ms tail for short responses, is that realistic with current kernels?

[12:37] Liam: Sub-50ms P95 for very short prompts is challenging at scale, but achievable for colocated runtimes with optimized batch windows and small-llm variants. For H100s you can get very low per-token latency — we'll validate in the benchmark. Also we can route latency-sensitive traffic to dedicated pools to avoid batching delays.

[13:05] Priya: Another practical ask — our pricing model is per-GPU-hour with a markup. Do you do per-token or per-inference pricing? How do we align?

[13:15] Maya: Redwood hosted is typically per-token for generation and per-embedding units for embeddings. For Dedicated/Private and reseller setups we have a hybrid: base infra fee (per GPU/hour or reserved capacity) plus per-token metering for optional cloud-managed services. We'll include pricing options in the SOW.

[13:38] [00:13:38] Maya: Let's sketch the pilot timeline quickly — onboarding (week 1), benchmark (week 2–3), integration test with a chosen customer (week 4–6), review and decision (week 7). Thoughts?
[13:52] Priya: That lines up with our target. Internally we want legal/compliance signoff before running customer-facing tests — that may add a week.

[14:10] Ethan: Concerning multi-tenant isolation — do you have workload cgroups or GPU partitioning to avoid noisy neighbors?

[14:20] Liam: We support workload isolation via GPU slices, MIG (for A100/H100 variants where applicable), and runtime cgroups. For strict tenancy we recommend dedicated GPU pools.

[14:45] Nina: Marketing/partnering note — if this goes well, Starlane is interested in co-branded go-to-market materials and a joint webinar.

[14:55] Maya: Love that. We do co-marketing with partners; we'll add that to the partnership brief.

[15:12] Priya: Any blackout for specific model licenses? Our customers sometimes want to run models with restrictive licenses.

[15:20] Liam: We don't enforce model licensing — that's typically between the customer and model vendor. We can support hosting almost any model artifact but will document any technical limitations.

[15:35] Ethan: For the benchmark, can we request a small sample of traffic patterns and a synthetic synthetic mix?

[15:43] Liam: Yes — send a sample prompt corpus and we will run it in an isolated environment and return latency/throughput/cost reports.

[16:05] [00:16:05] Priya: What about billing flow in a reseller model — does Redwood bill Starlane or the end-customer?

[16:13] Maya: We can do either. Common pattern is Redwood bills the reseller (Starlane) and Starlane bills the end-customer. We support billing exports and SSO-enabled invoices for transparency.

[16:32] Nina: Good to know. Also our legal team will want to see data processing addendums and SOC2 evidence — can you share those?

[16:40] Maya: Absolutely — I'll attach SOC2 and standard DPA in the follow-up.

[17:00] Ethan: A small deeper dive: does the runtime support autoscaling per-route? If a tenant suddenly spikes, can we autoscale only their pool?

[17:08] Liam: Autoscaling is both pool and route-aware. You can define autoscale policies for tenant pools or set burst capacity rules. We also support graceful fallback to a cheaper model variant if capacity is constrained.

[17:30] Priya: That's useful. How much effort to integrate your SDK into our provisioning flow? Our onboarding automation uses Terraform + Ansible.

[17:38] Liam: Minimal — the terraform modules and an operator are designed to be consumed by provisioning flows. If you share a sample terraform workflow I can propose a template.

[18:05] Maya: We should talk about a narrow pilot scope — what if we pick a single customer use-case (chat assistant for a SaaS customer) and run a head-to-head for 2 models: an open 13B model and a quantized 70B variant — benchmark throughput/latency/cost and K V cache behavior.

[18:28] Priya: I like that. We'll surface a candidate customer that is comfortable with pilot risk.

[18:40] Ethan: One more integration question — do you support service-mesh sidecars or do you require direct network paths?

[18:49] Liam: We can run behind service mesh sidecars; runtime exposes gRPC/HTTP endpoints compatible with sidecar routing. There may be TLS termination considerations but it's standard.

[19:10] Nina: Anything we should be worried about from Redwood's side? Known issues?

[19:16] Liam: On the tech side, a handful of custom ops or very unusual model topologies can require work. Other than that, most integration friction is networking and key management.

[19:35] Maya: Ok, let's capture next steps: I'll send SOW and partner margin sheet; Liam will send benchmark plan and perf spreadsheet; Ethan will send fleet inventory and sample prompt corpus; Priya will confirm pilot customer and legal contact.

[19:55] Priya: Sounds good. Timeline for those docs?

[19:58] Maya: SOW + margin sheet by 2026-07-20. Benchmark plan by 2026-07-16. Fleet inventory by 2026-07-17.

[20:15] [00:20:15] Maya: Are there any blockers to starting the pilot from Starlane's perspective?

[20:22] Priya: Just internal legal/compliance signoff and picking the pilot customer. On the tech side, no blockers.

[20:35] Ethan: We'll also want to run a small smoke test in a staging environment prior to customer testing.

[20:40] Liam: Agreed — we'll reserve a small staging pool.

[21:00] Nina: On commercial — initial question from our commercial team: can Redwood support white-labeling the UI and console for Starlane customers?

[21:08] Maya: We offer limited white-labeling for Dedicated/Private customers — logo and minor UI tweaks. Full white-labeling is an enterprise feature we can discuss for larger commitments.

[21:28] Priya: Last question — if performance regressions happen after an update, do you have rollout controls or automatic rollback?

[21:36] Liam: Yes, rollouts are canary/A-B with automatic rollback policies and gating based on evals and perf. You can pin model versions for tenants to avoid unexpected updates.

[22:00] Maya: Great. That wraps most of the technical and commercial questions. Any final points?

[22:08] Priya: No, just thanks — we'll consolidate internally and respond.
[22:12] Ethan: Thanks everyone.
[22:15] Nina: Thanks.
[22:18] Maya: Thanks — we'll send the docs and sync on the deep-dive next week.

Post-meeting notes (auto):
- Redwood to provide: SOW, reseller margin spreadsheet, SOC2 + DPA, terraform modules repo link, CIDR + port list, benchmark plan.
- Starlane to provide: fleet inventory (GPU types/nodes), sample prompt corpus, legal/compliance POC, candidate pilot customer.

References mentioned: Redwood Console demo, partner terraform modules (repo link placeholder: github.com/redwood/partner-terraform), pilot SOW template (doc link placeholder: drive.redwood/pilot-sow).
